headline: Build an AI-Powered Ad Blocker for Any Smart TV in 2024
summary: Learn how to build a local, AI-powered ad blocker for your Smart TV using a Raspberry Pi or NAS, eliminating ads without external services. This solution leverages lightweight LLMs and visual detection for real-time filtering, enhancing privacy and reducing ba
details: Tired of ad interruptions on your Smart TV? A new guide details how to build a local, AI-powered ad blocker. This solution utilizes lightweight LLMs like llama.cpp and Ollama, along with local APIs, to filter ads directly on your device.

The setup can run on low-cost edge devices such as a Raspberry Pi, a NAS, or even compatible Smart TVs that support Docker or Python scripts. This approach has seen a surge in interest, with "ad blocker smart tv" searches exploding on Google Trends.

By combining a local proxy, a lightweight LLM, and a TinyYOLO visual detector, you can eliminate ads from your Smart TV broadcasts without relying on external services. This method prioritizes user privacy and helps reduce bandwidth consumption.

The guide provides a comprehensive overview of the Smart TV advertising model, explains real-time detection technology, and offers a step-by-step tutorial with ready-to-use code. Users are encouraged to experiment and adjust parameters to their specific environment for an uninterrupted viewing experience.

headline_marked: [[Wired linked 149 Ikea $10 speakers]] to create a massive 447-watt wall of sound
headline: Wired linked 149 Ikea $10 speakers to create a massive 447-watt wall of sound
summary: Wired tested Ikea's claim of chaining 100 Kallsup Bluetooth speakers, successfully linking 149 of the $10 units to form a powerful, albeit "fire alarm loud," 447-watt sound system.
details: Ikea's $10 Kallsup Bluetooth speakers were advertised to chain up to 100 units. Wired pushed this limit, successfully linking 149 of the small cubes after one unit arrived faulty. This experiment created a literal wall of sound in their London office.

The chaining process was surprisingly simple: pair one speaker via Bluetooth 5.3 to a device, then power on additional Kallsup units and hold the Play button to enter multi-speaker mode. Each new speaker immediately joined the existing audio stream.

Individually, the Kallsup speakers, featuring a single 1.8-inch, 3-watt driver, offer decent sound for their price point. While lacking deep bass and prone to sounding "tinny" at high volumes, they perform well as small, portable desktop or travel speakers.

When combined, the 149 speakers delivered a surprisingly scaled sound, especially with acoustic tracks. The collective output, equivalent to a single 22-inch driver and 447 watts, resulted in an extremely loud experience, described as "fire alarm loud."

Despite the immense volume, the stacked wall of speakers remained stable, defying expectations of collapse due to vibrations. The experiment demonstrated the Kallsup's robust multi-speaker capability beyond Ikea's own tested limits.
